Granite. A coarse-grained, light-coloured felsic igneous rock composed primarily of quartz, feldspar, and mica. It forms deep underground from slow-cooling magma and is the most abundant intrusive igneous rock. Granites are highly prized as building stone and countertops because of their durability, aesthetic appeal, and resistance to weathering.

Granite is felsic, meaning it's high in feldspar and silica—about seventy percent silicon dioxide, much higher than basalt. It forms from slow cooling of magma deep underground, which allows large mineral crystals to grow. The mineral grains are visible to the naked eye because of that coarse-grained texture. The primary minerals are quartz, feldspar—both orthoclase and plagioclase—and mica, including muscovite and biotite, appearing in roughly equal proportions.

Granite is light-coloured, typically pink, white, or grey, due to its high content of light minerals like quartz and potassium feldspar, and its low iron and magnesium. It's less dense than basalt—around two point seven grams per cubic centimetre—and it's more chemically resistant to weathering because quartz is so stable. Granite comprises most of the continental crust and is exposed in mountain cores, shield regions, and eroded mountain belts.

Basalt is mafic—dark and low in silica—while granite is felsic and high in silica, representing opposite ends of igneous diversity. Orthoclase feldspar is a defining mineral of granite, appearing alongside plagioclase and quartz. Mica gives granite its characteristic sparkle and is a key identifying mineral. Granite is the prototypical intrusive igneous rock, cooled slowly beneath the surface, making it one of the most important rocks in understanding the Earth's structure.
